title: Guarding the City and Remembering Who Came Home
summary: With the wall finished, Nehemiah sets gatekeepers, singers, and Levites in place and appoints trustworthy men to guard Jerusalem. Seeing that the city is large but nearly empty, he gathers the people for enrollment and finds the register of the first exiles who returned from Babylon, which he copies out in full: lay families, towns, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, those who could not prove their descent, the totals, and the gifts given for the work.
story: The wall is built (chapter 6), but walls do not make a city. Jerusalem needs people, and Nehemiah's next task is to repopulate it, a task that will be completed in chapter 11 when a tenth of the people move into the city by lot. To prepare, he goes back to the beginning of the return from exile and reproduces the list of those who first came home, nearly a century before. The list is almost identical to Ezra 2. Its placement here ties Nehemiah's generation to the first returnees and sets up the great assembly of chapter 8, which begins in the seventh month mentioned in the list's final verse.
historical:
The register in verses 6-73 comes from the early days of the return. Cyrus the Great of Persia had conquered Babylon in 539 BC and allowed exiled peoples, including the Jews, to go home and rebuild their temples. The list names Zerubbabel, a descendant of King David who served as governor, and Jeshua (called Joshua in Haggai and Zechariah), the high priest, as leaders of the returning groups. The first returns probably took place over some years rather than in a single caravan, and the register may gather several waves together.

The list uses Persian-period terms. The official in verse 65 is called by a Persian title for a governor, and verses 70-72 count gifts in gold coins usually translated darics, the gold coin issued by the Persian kings from Darius I onward, though some scholars understand the Hebrew term as the Greek drachma. The mina was a larger unit of weight for silver. Nehemiah's own situation is sketched in verses 1-4: the walls stand and the gates are hung, but the houses inside are not yet rebuilt and few people live there.
cultural:
Gates in an ancient city were its weakest points, and Nehemiah's instructions in verse 3 reflect practical security: the gates stay closed until the sun is hot, well after dawn, so that no one could take the city in the early morning, and residents guard the sections near their own homes. The appointment of gatekeepers, singers, and Levites (verse 1) shows that the walled city was also the temple city, where worship and guarding went together.

Genealogy mattered deeply after the exile. The returning community was defined by descent from those who had been carried away, and the priesthood was limited by law to the descendants of Aaron. The families in verses 61-64 who could not document their lineage were not expelled from the people, but the priests among them were barred from eating the most holy portions until a priest could consult the Urim and Thummim, the sacred lots kept by the high priest for seeking God's decision (Exodus 28:30). The temple servants (verse 46) and the descendants of Solomon's servants (verse 57) were groups attached to the temple's service, probably descended in part from foreigners who had been brought into Israel's worship long before.
literary: The chapter has a short narrative frame (verses 1-5) around a long document (verses 6-73). The document is organized in categories: leaders (verse 7), lay families listed by clan (8-25) and by town (26-38), priests (39-42), Levites (43), singers (44), gatekeepers (45), temple servants and Solomon's servants (46-60), those of uncertain descent (61-65), totals of people and animals (66-69), and gifts (70-72). The final verse moves back into the story and leads straight into the assembly of chapter 8, much as the parallel list in Ezra 2 leads into the gathering of Ezra 3. Such lists were a normal part of ancient record-keeping, and here the list serves as a kind of family history for the whole community.

outline.t: Gatekeepers appointed and the city put under guard
An empty city and the register of the first returnees
The lay families and the men of the towns
Priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants
Families and priests who could not prove their descent
The totals of people and animals
Gifts for the work and settlement in the towns

doctrines.note: Nehemiah says, “Then my God put it into my heart to assemble the nobles, the officials, and the people” (verse 5). An administrative decision is described as God's prompting, a typical way Nehemiah understands God's guidance.

The list names people by family and town because God's promises were made to a people with a history. The returnees are shown to be the continuation of Israel, the same people God had chosen, now brought back to the land.

The priests who could not prove their descent were kept from the most holy things (verses 64-65). The care taken shows how seriously the community treated access to holy service, while the provision for a future decision by Urim and Thummim left the question open rather than closing it harshly.

words.note: Yachas, to enroll by genealogy. The verb describes registering people by family descent (verse 5), and the related noun is used for the register itself. After the exile, genealogical records were how a person proved membership in the community and, for priests, eligibility to serve.

Netinim, the temple servants, literally those given. They were a class of workers assigned to the temple's practical service, such as carrying wood and water. Their inclusion in the list shows that the restored community counted even its humblest servants by name.

Shoer, gatekeeper. Gatekeepers guarded the temple's entrances and, in this chapter, the city's gates as well (verse 1). The role joined security and holiness: keeping out what should not enter and protecting the worship within.

Qodesh, holiness or holy thing. In verse 65 the phrase “the most holy things” refers to the sacred portions of offerings reserved for priests. Holiness here means set apart for God, and the text treats that boundary with care.

christ: The link to Christ is thematic. The long list of names shows that God's purpose is carried by a real, named people with families and hometowns, and the Gospels open in the same way, with a genealogy that ties Jesus to Abraham and David (Matthew 1:1-17). The mention of Bethlehem among the towns of the returnees (verse 26) is a quiet reminder that the town of David's line was resettled and remained part of the story until the Messiah was born there. The New Testament also speaks of a book in which names are written (Luke 10:20; Revelation 21:27), and of Christ as the high priest whose standing does not depend on a human genealogy (Hebrews 7:16), but these are later developments of the theme rather than meanings hidden in this chapter.

hard.q: Why do the numbers in this list differ from the parallel list in Ezra 2?
hard.a:
Nehemiah 7:6-73 and Ezra 2:1-70 are clearly the same document, and both give a total of 42,360. But many of the individual family numbers differ slightly, a few names are spelled differently, and the individual figures do not add up to the total in either list (they come to about 31,089 in Nehemiah and 29,818 in Ezra). Interpreters explain this in several ways. Some think the two books preserve copies of the register made at different stages, one perhaps recording those who planned to go and the other those who arrived, or reflecting later updates. Others point to the known difficulty of copying numbers accurately in ancient manuscripts, since numerals and number words are easily confused. The gap between the parts and the total may mean the total includes people, such as women or others not counted by family, who are not listed separately.

None of these explanations is certain. What is clear is that the writers did not see the minor differences as a problem to be smoothed away, and that the list's purpose, to show who belonged to the restored community, is not affected by them.

questions: Nehemiah began repopulating Jerusalem by remembering who had come home before him. Why does a community of faith need to remember its own history?
Hananiah was chosen “because he was a faithful man who feared God more than most.” What qualities do you look for in people to whom you entrust something important?
The list includes priests and gatekeepers, landowners and temple servants. What does it say about God's people that all of them are named and counted?
